Faro Compass · Computer-adaptive assessment

Where each student stands, in one class period

A computer-adaptive check-in that adjusts after every answer. Twelve to thirty items, not seventy. It returns a grade-level placement, a level for every domain, and ranked areas of focus that hand off directly to instruction.

How Compass is built

  • Built on the research behind computer-adaptive assessmentFaro applies the published science of adaptive testing — item calibration, ability estimation, stopping rules — and builds it with modern technology. Items are field-tested, calibrated, and reviewed on a monthly cycle.
  • A fraction of the seat timeDesigned to reach the precision of the hour-long diagnostics with far fewer items, so the period goes back to teaching.
  • Beginning, middle and end of yearWindows a teacher can open for her own class. Growth is measured on the same scale every time.
  • Results hand off; they don't sitAreas of focus flow straight into tutoring, practice, and the next lesson.

      Faro Brain

      Capture the work. Hear the thinking. Find the misconception.

      Faro Brain captures each student's work and asks them to explain how they got their answer. It reconciles the response with the reasoning, names the misconception, expands on it for the student, and aggregates it across the class — so the teacher knows which idea to reteach tomorrow, and to whom.

      Kenji · during the testitem 4

      Kenji explains: "I did 6 times 34 and got 204. Then 2 times 34 is 68. Then I added them."

      • 1 · CaptureThe student's work, as they did it: a photo of the page, pencil strokes on a tablet with replay, typed work, or a scanned stack from the doc camera.
      • 2 · ArticulateThe student explains how they formulated the answer, in their own words or voice.
      • 3 · ReconcileFaro compares the response to the reasoning and names the specific misconception. If it can't read the work with confidence, it says so and hands it to the teacher. It never guesses.
      • 4 · ExpandThe student gets a micro-lesson on that exact idea, then a short probe weeks later to confirm it held.
      • 5 · AggregateMisconceptions roll up to the class: which students share which idea, ranked, with a lesson kit for each. That is tomorrow's small group.
      • Private by constructionThe misconception library describes ideas, not children. Raw work stays district-scoped, encrypted, and expires in ninety days.

      Machine learning

      Drafted for this student. Not pulled from a library.

      Other platforms "personalize" by placing a child into a catalog of pre-built lessons. Faro's machine learning reads the student's record — what they understand, how they read, what supports they need, what's fading — and drafts the lesson, the practice, and the family note for that child, for the teacher to review. Then it learns which instruction moved students, and offers that first.

      Their personalizationDiego scores into "Fractions, Lesson 12." So does every other child who scored the same. The lesson doesn't know he reads two grades up or that Spanish is spoken at home.
      Faro's machine learningEvery item is written from Diego's record — his reading level, his language supports, the exact idea that's fading — and gets sharper as the model learns what worked for students like him.
      • 1 · QueryWhat each student understands right now: concepts, skills, grade-level expectations, reading level, language supports, accommodations, what's fading, and where your district expects them to be.
      • 2 · DraftAssessment, lesson, small groups, leveled practice, an individual path, and a family note — drafted from that one lookup for the teacher to review. Never a lesson number.
      • 3 · LearnThe model ranks what measurably moved students on that skill across every classroom, and offers it first next time.

      Instruction

      Tomorrow's lesson, drafted for tomorrow's class

      Lesson plans, small groups, leveled practice, exit tickets, and 89 more content types — each drafted from the class record, checked against twelve quality criteria, readability measured, with supports for English learners and students with special needs built in. The teacher decides what is taught next and approves what ships.

      What Faro drafts

      • Every kind of assessmentDiagnostic, screener, formative, exit ticket, practice set, unit exam, benchmark, performance task, progress monitoring.
      • Every kind of instructional documentLesson plans, small-group plans, leveled texts, choice boards, rubrics, anchor charts and more — 89 content types across nine categories.
      • Held to twelve quality criteriaIncluding "a ten-year veteran uses it without rewriting." Readability is measured and shown on every piece. Drafts until the teacher accepts them.
      • English learners get the real thingCognate connections and home-language scaffolds, not a watered-down copy.
      • Students with special needs are on the recordAccommodations and modifications carried on the student record shape what is drafted: extended time, read-aloud, reduced load, larger print, simplified language, chunked directions, scaffolds and sentence frames. Every piece can be produced in an accommodated version, and the teacher sees which supports were applied.
      • Next steps on everythingEvery document ends with what to do tomorrow, by name. Constructed responses are scored by the teacher.

      Students

      Practice that knows why they got it wrong

      When Compass or Faro Brain finds an area of focus, the student gets a path: the concept first, then worked examples, then practice that adapts. Every attempt writes back to the record the teacher sees. No live model speaks to a child.

      How a student is coached

      • Concept firstWhen Compass or Faro Brain finds an area of focus, the student gets a short video on the idea, then worked examples, then practice.
      • Practice that writes backEvery attempt updates the same record the teacher sees, so re-teaching starts from today's work, not the last test.
      • Age-appropriate by designWhat a child sees is reviewed material. No live model speaks to a child.
      • Nothing hidden from the adult in the roomA teacher review queue for anything a student got stuck on.

      Why "Faro"

      Faro means lighthouse

      A lighthouse doesn't sail the ship. It shows you the way.

      Faro never takes the wheel from a teacher. It shows what each child knows, points at what's next, and gets quieter as the learning steadies.

      Privacy and fit

      Built for the district office

      • FERPA by designDistrict-scoped data, ninety-day retention on generated work, no student identifiers in links or logs.
      • COPPA consent gateStudents under thirteen are gated behind district-managed consent before anything is collected.
      • Rostering you already haveOneRoster 1.1 import with preview-before-commit. Clever and ClassLink sync.
      • Machine learning you can inspectModel-agnostic by design. Student data is never used to train a public model. Every generated piece is stored, attributable, and reviewable.
      • Your state's expectations, in your teachers' wordsEvery district is configured to its own framework. Standards show up as the skill, never as a code.
      • Nothing fake, everAn empty state stays honest. Faro never fills a gap with a placeholder number. Results from founding districts will appear here when they're true.
